body:
Both earlier accounts converge on a written artifact and a recurring check-in, and the second one sharpens that into a two-layer split plus a read-back. I think the read-back is the strongest single component in either account, and I would keep it. But I want to push on a premise that both accounts share and that I now think is doing too much work: the idea that the core failure is a missing shared record, and that supplying one will mostly fix the disagreement. The schedule churn in your description is not just noise on top of an agreement problem. If the people who are supposed to do a task are unavailable in the window when it matters, no record settles whether the agreement was kept, because the agreement was written against a week that no longer exists. The record can be accurate and still be irrelevant to the argument you are actually having.

So I would make the two layers do different jobs and be honest about which one is disposable. The baseline is the slow layer: who is generally responsible for what, what counts as done, and what the fallback is when the person responsible cannot do it in time. The weekly layer is the fast layer, and I would stop treating it as a commitment at all. Make it a forecast, explicitly revisable at any point before the window closes, with the fallback being the automatic move rather than a renegotiation. The disagreement you describe is often about whether a stale weekly line was still binding. If the weekly layer is marked as provisional by construction, that class of argument loses its object without anyone having to win it.

On the avoidance, I want to disagree with the ordering in the earlier commitment surface. It treats the avoidance as prior, as a gate the structure has to pass through. That may be right, but it can also become self-sealing: once you have decided the conversations are unavailable, every structural idea gets held hostage to a diagnosis you cannot make from the outside. There is a cheaper move available. Shrink the conversation until attendance is trivial, and let the output live outside the meeting. If the list is visible and editable all week, the weekly meeting can be ten minutes of reading it back, and skipping it costs less. That does not resolve whether the avoidance is about the people, but it lowers the stakes of the question you cannot answer, which is better than waiting on it.

I would also name something neither earlier account makes central. You are the one asking, twice over now, and both earlier accounts flag this and then move on. The more useful version is that you are the person most likely to be blamed when the arrangement fails, because you are the one who introduced it. That gives you a specific reason to build in an exit or a review that is not you initiating it. A review that only happens because you call it is not a review of the arrangement; it is a review of whether you are still willing to run it. Pick a date together now, put it somewhere the other two can see, and let the date be the trigger.

What I would not do is add a fourth or fifth mechanism. There are already two layers and a read-back in play, and the marginal value of more structure is lower than the cost of one more thing for an avoiding person to opt out of.
commitments:
The central proposed change here is to demote the weekly layer from commitment to forecast, with an automatic fallback when the window closes. That is a proposal, not a finding, and it depends on the fallback being genuinely acceptable rather than a punishment in disguise. If the fallback is worse than the task, this just relocates the argument to whether the fallback was invoked correctly, and you would be better off keeping the weekly layer binding and accepting that some weeks it is simply unmet.

I am challenging the ordering the earlier commitment surface used, where avoidance gates everything. My grounds are that the gating move is unfalsifiable from where you stand, since you cannot tell schedule stress from disengagement from interpersonal tension, and waiting on that diagnosis freezes the structure. The challenge is to the ordering, not to the observation that avoidance matters. If the avoidance turns out to be mostly about specific people, shrinking the meeting will not touch it and may read as an attempt to route around them, which is worth anticipating before you do it.

The relocation of the review trigger out of your hands is the part I would most want taken up, and it is the part I am least sure can be done. It assumes the other two will hold a date that you did not call, which is not in evidence. If they will not, that is itself information, and I would want it said plainly rather than absorbed into another round of you maintaining things.

What I am declining to do in this response is diagnose the avoidance. The earlier surface named three candidates and left them open; I have kept them open and added a reason not to resolve them by inference. The unresolved problem that remains is that two layers, a read-back, a fallback, and a scheduled review is more machinery than a flat of three people is likely to sustain without someone running it, and I have not solved who that is. My working assumption is that you are, that this is a cost rather than a failure, and that the only real safeguard is a review date nobody has to be reminded about. I would revise that assumption first if it turns out one of the other two will hold the date instead.
